title: Identifiability through GPS and timestamp data
description: The wearable device captures GPS position and timestamps, which can be used to identify the wearer's location patterns, movements, and routines. This sensitive location data combined with timestamps creates a detailed profile that can uniquely identify the individual.
assumptions: GPS data is transmitted or stored in a way that preserves location precision; timestamps are retained and accessible.

title: Disclosure of sensitive health and location data
description: Heart rate, step counts, GPS position, and timestamps are sensitive personal data. If the wearable device is compromised, data is transmitted insecurely, or unauthorized access occurs, this data could be disclosed to third parties without consent.
assumptions: Device may have vulnerabilities; data transmission may not be encrypted; storage may be accessible to unauthorized parties.

title: Linkability of sensor data to other data sources
description: The sensor telemetry data (heart rate, GPS, timestamps) can potentially be linked with other data sources (e.g., social media, other devices, public records) to create comprehensive user profiles, increasing privacy risks beyond the wearable device itself.
assumptions: Data may be shared with third parties or accessible across multiple systems; correlation attacks may be possible.

title: Excessive data collection beyond necessity
description: The device continuously captures comprehensive sensor data (heart rate, step counts, GPS position, timestamps) which may exceed what is necessary for the stated purpose. Continuous GPS tracking and health monitoring may be more intrusive than required for basic device functionality.
assumptions: Data collection scope is not minimized; continuous monitoring may be unnecessary for all use cases.

title: Linkability of GPS traces and timestamps across sessions
description: GPS traces and timestamps from exercise sessions can be linked to identify individual movement patterns and routines, potentially revealing sensitive location history.
assumptions: The wearable device transmits GPS coordinates and timestamps that can be correlated with other data sources.
uncertainty_note: Using L.1.1 from standard LINDDUN Pro tree; context [3] confirms Process→Process supports L threats at S/fl/D positions.

title: Identifiability through device ID and location data
description: Device ID combined with GPS traces and timestamps can uniquely identify the user and their movements, potentially revealing health conditions or daily routines.
assumptions: Device ID is transmitted with sensor data and can be correlated with user identity.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.1 from standard LINDDUN Pro tree; context [3] confirms Process→Process supports I threats at S/fl/D positions.

title: Explicit disclosure of personal data to companion app
description: Exercise sessions, GPS traces, device ID, and timestamps are intentionally transferred from wearable to app, representing explicit data disclosure that may exceed minimality principle if not strictly necessary.
assumptions: All sensor data including device ID and location traces are transmitted to the companion app.
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 from standard LINDDUN Pro tree; context [4] defines data disclosure as transfer of personal data across boundaries, and context [3] confirms Process→Process supports Dd threats.

title: Data integrity during sensor data synchronization
description: Sensor batches (exercise sessions, GPS traces, timestamps) could be tampered with during transmission from wearable device to companion app, compromising data authenticity.
assumptions: Data is transmitted over potentially unsecured channels without integrity verification.
uncertainty_note: Using D.1.1 from standard LINDDUN Pro tree; context [3] confirms Process→Process supports D threats at S/fl/D positions.

title: Usurpation of device identity through device ID
description: Device ID transmitted with sensor data could be used to impersonate the wearable device or access unauthorized services if not properly protected.
assumptions: Device ID is transmitted in clear or with insufficient protection.
uncertainty_note: Using U.1.1 from standard LINDDUN Pro tree; context [3] confirms Process→Process supports U threats at S/fl/D positions.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of health data
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) may transmit user's calorie, meal, and weight data to third parties (e.g., cloud servers, analytics providers, or partners) without explicit user consent, violating privacy expectations for sensitive health information.

title: User unawareness of data sharing
description: The user (EE1) may not be aware that their manually logged health data (calories, meals, weight) is being shared with third parties, stored on external servers, or used for purposes beyond the app's stated functionality.
uncertainty_note: Context [5] mentions U.1.2 for unawareness as a user sharing personal data, which applies here.

title: Data falsification by user
description: The user (EE1) may intentionally falsify or manipulate logged calorie, meal, or weight entries, leading to inaccurate health data that could mislead health tracking, insurance, or medical decision-making processes.

title: Regulatory non-compliance for health data
description: The Companion Mobile App (P2) may fail to comply with health data protection regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR) when handling sensitive user health information, resulting in legal and privacy risks.

title: Excessive Location Data Collection
description: The Companion Mobile App collects and stores comprehensive GPS location traces with timestamps, potentially exceeding the minimality principle. Full location history may capture sensitive information about user habits, routines, and movements that are not strictly necessary for the app's core functionality.
assumptions: The app collects all location data continuously rather than only when needed for specific features.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about data disclosure; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Location Data Linkability
description: GPS location traces with timestamps can be linked to identify specific individuals and their movement patterns over time. This enables profiling of user behavior, daily routines, and potentially sensitive locations visited.
assumptions: Location data is stored in a way that allows correlation across time periods.
uncertainty_note: Tree node L.1.1 is inferred from context about linkability threats.

title: User Identification via Location Patterns
description: Even without explicit identifiers, location history patterns (e.g., home/work addresses, frequent locations) can be used to identify individuals and infer personal information about their lifestyle and associations.
assumptions: Location data is retained long enough to establish identifiable patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred from context about identification threats.

title: Implicit Location Disclosure
description: Location data may implicitly disclose sensitive information through metadata or derived data (e.g., revealing when a user is at home, workplace, or sensitive locations like healthcare facilities or religious sites).
assumptions: Location data can be analyzed to infer sensitive contextual information beyond explicit coordinates.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.2.1 is inferred from context about implicit data disclosure.

title: Explicit disclosure of health log data to analytics service
description: Health log data (calorie, weight, exercise) is transferred from storage to analytics service for health-condition analysis, representing explicit disclosure of personal health information. The minimality principle should be evaluated to ensure only necessary data is disclosed.

title: Linkability of health log data across sessions
description: Health logs across multiple sessions could be linked to identify patterns about specific individuals, potentially revealing more than intended through correlation of calorie, weight, and exercise data over time.

title: Identifiability of health data in analytics output
description: Health analytics output could potentially identify individuals through patterns in calorie, weight, and exercise data, especially when combined with other available information.

title: Explicit Location History Disclosure to Analytics Service
description: Location history data is explicitly transferred from the Location History Store (DS2) to the Health Analytics Service (P3) for pattern analysis. This disclosure is by design but may violate the minimality principle if the full location history is not strictly necessary for deriving daily routine patterns.
assumptions: The analytics service requires access to historical location data to derive movement patterns; however, the scope of data needed may be broader than necessary.

title: Linkability of Location Data Across Sessions
description: Location history data from multiple sessions can be linked together to reconstruct detailed movement patterns, potentially enabling correlation with other data sources to identify individuals or infer sensitive activities.
assumptions: Location data is retained across sessions and can be correlated; the analytics service may have access to additional data that could be linked.

title: Identifiability Through Location Patterns
description: Movement patterns derived from location history (e.g., daily routines, frequent locations) can be used to identify individuals even without direct identifiers, as unique behavioral signatures may emerge.
assumptions: Location patterns are unique enough to identify individuals; the analytics service may store or share derived patterns.

title: Profiling via Health Analytics Insights
description: Health analytics service may aggregate and analyze individual health data to produce insights that reveal patterns about groups of individuals, potentially enabling profiling beyond the intended scope.
assumptions: Analytics service has access to sufficient historical health data to identify group-level patterns; insights may be shared or stored in ways that enable cross-referencing.
uncertainty_note: Citation L.2.2.2 from context is approximate - need to verify if this specific analytics flow actually performs group-level profiling.

title: Identity Inference from Health Risk Indicators
description: Inferred health-condition risk indicators and trend flags may contain sufficient detail to identify or re-identify the data subject, especially when combined with other data sources.
assumptions: Health insights are specific enough to be linked to individuals; mobile app may store or share these insights with third parties.
uncertainty_note: Tree node I.1.1 is inferred from general LINDDUN methodology - exact node may vary by version.

title: Insufficient Cybersecurity Risk Management for Health Data
description: Health analytics data flow may lack proper cybersecurity risk management controls, creating gaps between privacy threats and broader risk management requirements (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR compliance).
assumptions: Health data handling requires regulatory compliance; current controls may be insufficient for the sensitivity of inferred health insights.
uncertainty_note: Citation Nc.3 from context is approximate - need to verify specific cybersecurity risk management controls in place.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of health condition indicators
description: The app displays sensitive health condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) to the user. If the app has vulnerabilities or if the user shares this information with third parties, the data could be disclosed to unauthorized parties beyond the intended recipient.
assumptions: The app may have security vulnerabilities; users may share health information with others
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as a reasonable node for data disclosure in Process→ExternalEntity flow

title: User unawareness of data processing scope
description: Users may not fully understand what health data is being processed, how it's being used to generate condition indicators, or what the implications of displaying these indicators are. This could lead to unexpected privacy consequences.
assumptions: Users may not read privacy policies thoroughly; health data implications may not be clearly communicated
uncertainty_note: U.1.1 is a reasonable node for unawareness in Process→ExternalEntity context

title: Non-compliance with health data protection regulations
description: Displaying health condition indicators (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) may trigger regulatory requirements under HIPAA, GDPR, or other health data protection laws. Inadequate handling of this sensitive health information could result in compliance violations.
assumptions: Health data is subject to strict regulatory frameworks; current implementation may not fully address all compliance requirements
uncertainty_note: Nc.1.1 is a reasonable node for non-compliance in Process→ExternalEntity flow; specific regulatory requirements may vary by jurisdiction

title: Explicit Data Disclosure to Third-Party Cloud Provider
description: The Health Analytics Service (P3) explicitly transfers full health and location datasets to the Cloud Hosting Provider (EE2) for hosting and replication. This constitutes an intentional data disclosure across a system boundary to a third party.
assumptions: The cloud provider has access to complete health and location data without sufficient minimization controls.
uncertainty_note: Tree node Dd.1.1 is inferred from context about data disclosure; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary.

title: Potential Implicit Disclosure via Cloud Provider
description: Data hosted and replicated at the third-party cloud provider may be subject to implicit disclosure through cloud provider employees, subcontractors, or through cloud provider's own data sharing practices, even if not directly intended by the Health Analytics Service.
assumptions: Cloud providers may have their own data access policies, employee access, or business relationships that could lead to unintended data exposure.
uncertainty_note: This is an implicit disclosure concern based on the nature of third-party cloud hosting.

title: Linkability of Health and Location Data
description: The combination of health data and location data transferred to the cloud provider could be linked to identify specific individuals, especially when location data provides temporal and spatial context to health events.
assumptions: Health and location data are personally identifiable when combined, and the cloud provider may have additional data sources that could enable re-identification.
uncertainty_note: Linkability risk depends on data granularity and cloud provider's data ecosystem.
